claims.text: Increasing aluminum content or activity relative to chromium in CrFeCoNiX alloys promotes formation of a protective oxide above 900 °C.
The promoted protective oxide is selectively formed Al2O3.
Al2O3 scales grow more slowly than chromium oxide scales and are more stable in aggressive high-temperature environments.
An Al2O3 scale on these alloys is coherent and adheres well to the substrate.
A continuous Al2O3 layer inhibits further oxygen ingress.
Chromium diffuses outward faster than oxygen diffuses inward during chromia-scale growth.
Above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3.
Formation of Al2O3 suppresses rapid chromium outward diffusion and CrO3 volatilization.
Suppressing chromium transport and volatilization reduces internal stresses that cause oxide cracking and spallation.
Chromium in lower relative amounts tends to form volatile CrO3 at high temperatures.
Volatile chromium oxide causes rapid scale growth and stress accumulation.
The Al/Cr ratio governs interfacial stress and diffusion kinetics controlling cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNiX alloys with an enhanced Al/Cr ratio will retain a stable, slow-growing Al2O3 layer with minimized cracking and spallation during prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
Alloys with insufficient aluminum or excessive chromium will primarily form volatile chromium oxides and mixed oxides that produce unstable, crack-prone scales.
A lower-aluminum or higher-relative-chromium baseline is expected to crack and spall more than the enhanced-Al/Cr alloy.
A Cr-Mn-Fe-Co FCC alloy develops surface cracks and oxide spallation after oxidation at 900 °C.
The proposed relationship is valid across the studied CrFeCoNiX composition range in oxidative or corrosive environments above 900 °C.
Si, Mn, and multiphase microstructures may influence phase distribution and oxide adherence or growth kinetics.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says chromium in lower relative amounts tends to form volatile CrO3, whereas the predicted outcome and baseline associate excessive or higher relative chromium with volatile, unstable chromium oxides.

The alloy scope defines X as one of Si, Mn, or Al, but the intervention proposes varying Al while keeping Si and Mn constant. For X = Si or Mn this introduces an additional element and no longer describes the stated CrFeCoNiX quinary formulation.
